who: a great German port city
why: Ships out of the port carried a minced beef dish that took the city's name.
mean: A patty of minced beef served in a bun
story: Sailors leaving one busy German port ate a minced beef steak served flat on a plate. They carried the habit across the Atlantic, cooks there slid the patty into a bun, and the sandwich kept the port city's name.

who: an American president and keen hunter (1858-1919)
why: He refused to shoot a tethered bear, and a cartoon of the moment inspired a toymaker.
mean: A soft stuffed toy bear
story: On a hunting trip a president refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree, calling it unsporting. A newspaper cartoon spread the story, a shopkeeper sewed a plush bear in tribute, and the toy carried his nickname ever after.

who: an English boarding school
why: The handling game grew up in that school's playing fields and took its name.
mean: A team sport played with an oval ball that players may carry
story: At one English school the football rules allowed a player to pick the ball up and run with it. Old boys carried the handling version to clubs everywhere, and to tell it apart from the kicking game people simply called it by the school's name.

who: a coastal region on the Adriatic
why: The spotted coach dog was associated with that coast and named for it.
mean: A white dog covered in black or brown spots
story: A tall spotted dog that loved to trot beside horses became fashionable as a carriage escort. Early writers linked the breed to one stretch of Adriatic coastline, and although the connection is thin, the region's name stuck to the dog for good.

who: a rugged region of eastern Canada
why: The water dog came from the coast of that region.
mean: A strong, friendly retriever with a short water-shedding coat
story: Fishermen on a cold Canadian coast kept short-haired dogs that dived into freezing water after nets and fish. English gentlemen brought the dogs home, bred them for the shooting field, and named them after the coast they came from.

who: the largest state in Mexico
why: The tiny dog was first noticed by travellers in that state.
mean: A very small dog with large upright ears
story: American visitors to a northern Mexican state in the 1800s bought tiny dogs from villagers near the border. Nobody recorded a breed name, so the buyers simply used the name of the state, and the smallest dog in the world has answered to it since.

who: the ancient empire of modern Iran
why: Romans thought the fruit came from there and called it the Persian apple.
mean: A soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large stone
story: The fruit really began in China, but it reached Rome along the road from Persia. Roman growers called it the Persian apple, persicum, and centuries of shortening in French wore that long name down to a single soft syllable.

who: a highland region of Ethiopia
why: The wild coffee plant grows there, and the drink's name traces back through Arabic to it.
mean: A hot drink brewed from roasted ground beans
story: Wild bushes with red berries still grow in one Ethiopian highland. Traders carried the beans to Arabia, where the brewed drink became qahwa, and every European name for it -- cafe, kaffee and the English word -- goes back to that first green hillside.

who: the Greek titan of the world-encircling river
why: Greeks pictured a vast river running round the edge of the earth and named it after him.
mean: A very large expanse of salt water
story: Greeks imagined the earth as a flat disc ringed by one endless river, and gave that river the name of a titan, the eldest son of sky and earth. When sailors learned the water went on much further than they thought, the titan's name went with it.

who: sea creatures in Greek myth whose singing lured sailors onto rocks
why: A warning device that wails was named after the singers whose voices meant danger.
mean: A device that makes a loud wailing warning sound
story: In the old story, singers on a rocky island sang so beautifully that crews steered towards them and were wrecked. Odysseus tied himself to the mast to hear them safely. Centuries later an inventor gave the name to a machine whose wail means danger.

who: the ash-covered heroine of a fairy tale retold by Charles Perrault
why: Her sudden rise from drudgery to glory became the name for any such transformation.
mean: Someone overlooked who suddenly rises to success
story: A girl who slept beside the fireplace and was named for the cinders in her clothes went to the ball and left one slipper behind. Now any unfancied team that reaches the final, or any ignored talent that shines, gets called by her name.

who: the girl in the tale of the three bears
why: Her habit of rejecting extremes and choosing the middle option became a scientific shorthand.
mean: Neither too much nor too little; just right
story: A girl in a fairy tale tried porridge too hot, then too cold, then just right. Astronomers borrowed her fussiness: a planet in the narrow band that is neither too hot nor too cold for water now sits in the zone named for her.

who: the boy who would not grow up, created by J. M. Barrie
why: His refusal to age became the name for adults who never quite do either.
mean: An adult who refuses to grow up
story: A playwright invented a boy who flew, fought pirates, and flatly refused to get any older. Psychologists later borrowed him: someone who dodges every adult responsibility and stays a delighted child is said to have his syndrome.

who: the tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
why: His riddles and wild manner made his name a byword for cheerful nonsense.
mean: A person who behaves in a wildly eccentric way
story: At a tea party that never ended, a hat-maker asked a riddle he could not answer and poured tea on a dormouse. Real hat-makers of the day were poisoned by the mercury they used, which is why madness and hat-making went together in the joke.

who: the grinning cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
why: It faded away leaving only its grin, so its name attaches to any wide fixed smile.
mean: A broad fixed grin
story: A cat in a wonderland book sat in a tree, gave unhelpful directions, and vanished slowly from the tail forwards until nothing was left but its grin. Anyone smiling that widely for no clear reason is now said to be grinning like it.

who: the egg who sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme
why: Because he could not be put back together, his name means anything broken beyond repair.
mean: Something so broken it cannot be mended
story: An egg sat on a wall, fell off, and all the king's horses and men could do nothing about it. Writers now reach for his name whenever a treaty, a company or a friendship has shattered in a way no committee is going to fix.

who: a small town in eastern Belgium
why: Its iron-rich springs drew visitors from all over Europe, and the town's name became the word for any such resort.
mean: A resort with mineral springs or health treatments
story: A Belgian town with bubbling iron-rich springs became the fashionable place to take the waters in the 1500s. Visitors came home saying they had been to the town by name, and soon every mineral bath in Europe was borrowing it.

who: the large Mediterranean island
why: The little fish were caught in huge numbers off its coast.
mean: A small oily fish often packed tightly in tins
story: Fishing boats around one large Mediterranean island hauled in silver shoals of a small oily fish by the tonne. The catch was salted, shipped and eventually tinned, and it carried the island's name to breakfast tables everywhere.

who: a stately home in Gloucestershire, England
why: Guests of the duke played the shuttlecock game in its great hall.
mean: A racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net
story: Officers home from India brought back a shuttlecock game and played it in the hall of an English duke's country house on a wet afternoon. When people asked what the game was called, they answered with the name of the house.

who: an American bridge engineer (1859-1896)
why: He built the giant rotating wheel for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.
mean: A giant upright rotating wheel with passenger cars
story: Chicago wanted something to outdo the Eiffel Tower. A bridge engineer proposed a wheel two hundred and fifty feet across, carrying two thousand people at once. Everyone said it would collapse; it did not, and every big wheel since has borne his name.

who: the land the stone was traded through
why: The blue-green stone reached Europe by Turkish traders, so French called it the Turkish stone.
mean: A blue-green mineral, or that colour
story: The blue-green stone was mined in Persia, but it reached Venice and Paris in the packs of Turkish merchants. French buyers called it pierre turquoise, the Turkish stone, and the shortened word now names the colour as much as the mineral.

who: a town in the Mexican state of Jalisco
why: The blue agave spirit is distilled in and around it.
mean: A Mexican spirit distilled from blue agave
story: In the red volcanic soil around one Mexican town, blue agave plants grow for years before their hearts are roasted and distilled. Mexican law now says the spirit may only carry the town's name if it comes from that region.

who: a historic region on the Baltic coast
why: The tiny fluffy dog was bred down from larger sled dogs of that region.
mean: A very small long-haired dog with a plumed tail
story: Big white spitz dogs pulled sleds along a cold Baltic coast. Breeders shrank them generation by generation until Queen Victoria fell for an eleven-pound one and made the miniature fashionable, and the region's name shrank onto the little dog.

who: a town in south-west Germany
why: Butchers there used the powerful dogs to drive cattle and guard money.
mean: A large powerful black-and-tan guard dog
story: Butchers in a German market town used heavy dogs to drive cattle to market, then tied the purse of takings round the dog's neck for the walk home. Nobody robbed them. The town's name went onto the breed and stayed.

who: the old name of Thailand
why: The pale cat with dark points was first brought to the West from the Siamese royal court.
mean: A slender pale cat with dark face, ears, paws and tail
story: A pair of pale blue-eyed cats with sooty faces was given to a British consul by a royal court in South East Asia in 1884. They were shown in London the next year, astonished everybody, and took the kingdom's old name as their own.

who: a stretch of West African coast
why: The South American rodent reached Europe on ships from that trade route and picked up the wrong continent's name.
mean: A small tailless rodent kept as a pet or used in experiments
story: The animal is not a pig and has never been near West Africa: it comes from the Andes. But it arrived in Europe aboard ships working the Guinea trade route, sailors named it after the last coast they had seen, and the mistake stuck.

who: a port on the Red Sea coast of Yemen
why: The world's coffee once shipped from that harbour.
mean: A rich coffee, or coffee flavoured with chocolate
story: For two hundred years almost every coffee bean that reached Europe left through one Yemeni harbour. The beans had a chocolatey edge, so when cooks later stirred cocoa into coffee they reached for the harbour's name to describe it.

who: the main island of Indonesia
why: Dutch plantations there supplied so much coffee that the island's name became slang for the drink.
mean: Coffee
story: Dutch growers planted coffee across one Indonesian island until it supplied much of the world. American sailors and soldiers took to calling any cup of coffee by the island's name, and a programming language later borrowed it as a nod to the coders' fuel.

who: the capital of Peru
why: The bean was exported from that port in boxes stamped with the city's name.
mean: A flat pale edible bean
story: Crates of a broad flat bean left a Peruvian port stamped with the city of origin. Buyers in North America read the stamp rather than any botanical label, and started ordering the beans by the name of the city instead.

who: an Australian orchardist (1799-1870)
why: A chance seedling on her farm produced the hard green apple.
mean: A hard, tart, bright green apple
story: An Australian orchardist threw some French crab apple cores onto a creek bank. A seedling came up, and its fruit turned out hard, sharp and green, and kept for months. Neighbours called it by her nickname and the apple never lost it.

who: a Scottish-Australian chemist and doctor (1827-1865)
why: A botanist friend named the Australian nut tree in his honour.
mean: A hard-shelled Australian nut with rich creamy flesh
story: A botanist studying rainforest trees in Queensland found one with a nut so hard you needed a hammer. He named the genus after a chemist friend who, as it happens, never tasted the nut that would carry his name around the world.

who: an Omaha grocer (1873-1960)
why: He is credited with building the grilled corned-beef sandwich during a weekly poker game.
mean: A grilled sandwich of corned beef, sauerkraut, cheese and dressing on rye
story: A grocer playing his weekly poker game in an Omaha hotel asked the kitchen for corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and dressing between rye bread, grilled. The hotel owner put it on the menu under the player's first name, and it never came off.

who: the French emperor (1769-1821)
why: The layered pastry's French name, napolitain, drifted into the emperor's name in English.
mean: A layered pastry of puff pastry and cream
story: The layered cream slice began as a Naples pastry, napolitain in French. English speakers heard the more famous name in it and rewrote the word, so the dessert now honours an emperor who had nothing whatever to do with inventing it.

who: a city in northern Italy famous for its cooking
why: The slow-cooked meat sauce is the city's signature dish.
mean: A slow-cooked Italian meat and tomato sauce
story: Cooks in one wealthy northern Italian city simmered minced meat with a little tomato, milk and wine for hours, and served it with wide flat pasta. The city's name travelled with the recipe, though what most countries make of it would horrify the locals.

who: a southern Italian port city
why: Ice cream sellers from the city introduced the three-flavour brick abroad.
mean: Ice cream in three coloured layers
story: Ice cream makers from a southern Italian port emigrated in the 1800s and sold moulded ice cream in coloured stripes, in imitation of their national flag. Abroad the layers became chocolate, vanilla and strawberry, and kept the city's name.

who: a port city in south-west France
why: The red wine of the surrounding vineyards is shipped from and named for it.
mean: A red wine from the region around one French port
story: For centuries English merchants bought red wine at one French Atlantic port and shipped it home in barrels. They called it by the harbour rather than the vineyard, and even now the region's most famous wines answer to the port's name.

who: the country the dye was traded from
why: Greeks called the deep blue dye the Indian substance.
mean: A deep blue-violet dye or colour
story: Greek traders met a deep blue dye that came in hard cakes from the East, and called it indikon, simply the Indian thing. The name outlasted the trade: the colour between blue and violet in the rainbow still carries the country's name.

who: the Mediterranean island whose mines supplied Rome
why: Romans called the metal aes cyprium, the metal of Cyprus.
mean: A soft reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity well
story: Rome got most of its reddish metal from mines on one Mediterranean island, and called it the Cyprus metal. Latin wore aes cyprium down to cuprum, and English wore that down again, so an island's name now sits in every electrical cable.

who: a border region between France and Germany
why: British breeders renamed the German shepherd after the region during the First World War.
mean: A large German shepherd dog
story: During the First World War British owners could not bring themselves to call the breed a German shepherd. They renamed it after a border region that had changed hands between the two countries, and in Britain the wartime alias lasted for decades.

who: the old English name for Beijing
why: The flat-faced dogs were bred in the Chinese imperial palace and taken from it in 1860.
mean: A small flat-faced dog with a long flowing coat
story: Only the Chinese imperial family could keep the little lion dogs of the palace. When British and French troops looted the Summer Palace in 1860 five were carried off, one was given to Queen Victoria, and the capital's old name went with them.

who: the peninsula where the breed was developed
why: Bedouin tribes bred the horse for endurance in the desert.
mean: A horse breed with a dished face, high tail and great stamina
story: Desert tribes bred horses that could go far on little water and live close to the family tent. The line is one of the oldest kept anywhere, and almost every modern racing breed carries some of its blood along with the peninsula's name.

who: the many-headed water serpent of Greek myth
why: Cutting off one head grew two, so any problem that multiplies when attacked takes its name.
mean: A problem that grows worse each time you attack it
story: Heracles found that every head he sliced off the marsh serpent was replaced by two more, and only fire could stop the regrowth. Ever since, a difficulty that spawns two new difficulties each time you solve it has been called by the monster's name.

who: the great serpent of Delphi killed by Apollo
why: Naturalists borrowed the myth-serpent's name for the huge constricting snakes.
mean: A large snake that kills by constriction
story: A monstrous serpent guarded the spring at Delphi until Apollo shot it, and the oracle's priestess took her title from it. When naturalists needed a name for enormous constricting snakes, they reached back into the myth for the serpent's own.

who: the Roman goddess of the dawn
why: The glowing polar lights were named for the goddess who coloured the morning sky.
mean: The coloured lights that glow in polar skies
story: Romans said a goddess rose each morning to paint the eastern sky before the sun came up. When Galileo needed a name for the green and red curtains that hang over the far north, he gave them hers, adding the northern dawn.

who: the Roman goddess and personification of the moon
why: Madness was believed to come and go with the phases of the moon.
mean: A person behaving wildly or foolishly
story: Doctors from Rome to the Middle Ages believed that fits of madness rose and fell with the phases of the moon, and English law once separated the permanently ill from those thought to change with it. The moon goddess's name is still inside the word.

who: the unseen ruler in George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: His name became shorthand for a state that watches everything its citizens do.
mean: Constant surveillance by an authority
story: In a novel published in 1949 every wall carried a poster of a moustached face and the line that he was watching you. Nobody in the book ever meets him. Seventy years on, his name is the fastest way to say a state is watching too closely.
